title: Beyond Tomorrow

evidence.note: The Internet Archive metadata gives a release date of May 10, 1940. It says the uploader asserts the work is in the public domain. A 1940 US film is free only if its notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. I fetched the Stanford renewal database search page again in this session and it returned no usable content. I did not read the 1967-1969 Catalog of Copyright Entries volumes, so I cannot cite a renewal-absence result. The uploader's public domain claim is not a rights determination. Check the 1967-1969 renewal window by hand.
This is a sound film. The recorded track normally shares the film's own copyright status, so the score is undetermined for the same reason as the print. I found no separate music-copyright record.
evidence.source: Internet Archive item page for the 1940 film

evidence.note: The Internet Archive metadata credits an original story by Mildred Cram and Adele Comandini, with a screenplay by Adele Comandini. I did not research whether the story was published separately or when, so its term is unconfirmed.

The Internet Archive page says a colorized version was produced by Legend Films in 2004 and released by 20th Century Fox as 'Beyond Christmas'. It also says the original black-and-white print was digitally remastered and preserved by the National Film Museum, Incorporated. A faithful black-and-white copy adds no new US copyright. The colorization, and any added material, can carry its own protection.

editorial:
Beyond Tomorrow is a 1940 fantasy directed by A. Edward Sutherland and produced by cinematographer Lee Garmes, with an original story credited to Mildred Cram and Adele Comandini and a screenplay by Adele Comandini. Three elderly industrialists die in a plane crash and return as ghosts to help reunite a young couple. Its Christmas setting is why people look for a free copy.

A 1940 film is free in the US only if its copyright notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. I could not confirm either from a primary record, so every layer except restorations is undetermined. The renewal catalogs for 1967 to 1969 are the place to check. The trap is the colorized edition: Legend Films colorized the film and 20th Century Fox released it in 2004 as 'Beyond Christmas'. That colorization is a separate layer and should not be assumed free, even if the black-and-white original turns out to be.
faq: Is Beyond Tomorrow (1940) free to use?

Not confirmed. It is a 1940 film, so it is free only if its notice was missing or its copyright was not renewed. I could not verify either from a primary record. Check the 1967-1969 renewal catalogs using the links in the dossier. The uploader's public-domain claim on the Internet Archive is not a rights determination.
Can I use the colorized version of Beyond Tomorrow?

Use a black-and-white print instead. The Internet Archive page says Legend Films produced a colorized version, released by 20th Century Fox in 2004 as 'Beyond Christmas'. The colorization can be separately protected even if the original film is free.
